title: Part 2
text: like it had personally insulted him. "Right," he sighed, mostly to himself, running a hand back through his hair as he looked around the small room. Dwight was doing his level best not to climb out of his own skin against the far wall. David filed that away and did the math. Go back. Check if Danny had moved on. It was the sensible option — retrace through the pipe hallway, find the first room, see if the stairwell was clear. Simple. Logical. Except that the hallway had somehow doubled in length on their first pass through it, the flashlight had about as much range as a lit match, and the water was still rising with absolutely no indication that it intended to stop. Going back meant navigating all of that in the dark, on a maybe, with no guarantee that anything had changed. It was clearly a bad idea. So was staying where they were and fighting with the immovable wall of furniture. Though... “I mean...” he said, voice low and edged. “...there IS a plan B.” The sound of his boots dragging through the water was louder than the voice in his head telling him this was a bad idea. David scrubbed a hand through his hair, flicking water off his fingers in frustration. Dwight hunched in on himself, flinching again as something bumped his calf for the umpteenth time. He didn’t even bother to hiss a warning this time, just shot a glare into the shadows, flashlight beam jittering with the tremor in his hand. “There’s always the ceiling hole in the pipe hall.” Dwight stared at him like he'd been punched. “The pipe hall?” His voice cracked. “We barely made it through the first time, and now it’s half- flooded and pitch black. Getting past it is one thing, but you want to search it?! What if we miss the hole? What if it’s gone?” “It’s not,” David said, too quickly. Too certain. “But...” “Look, I don’t like it either. But we don’t really have time here. Plus, it’s dark enough that we wouldn’t be seen climbing out into the main hallway.” “David, it’s almost 8 feet up! You might be able to climb that...” Dwight froze as a look of tense guilt washed over David. In a heartbeat, he realized what David was hinting at. “You want to wait out the flood. Let the water get us up there.” Dwight watched his jaw tense as he turned his eyes away. It was a bad decision, clearly. But so was everything else. If Ghostface was still at the other stairs, they wouldn’t see him in time. If they kept trying at these stairs, they would loose precious time needed to search the pipe hallway. Assuming they DID find the hole, they would need to wait out the rising water in the dark. No option felt good, but at least the ceiling hole had less chance of getting them stabbed. Dwight looked at the water sitting dark and patient at his waist, and felt something cold move through him regardless. “God, I hate that that might actually work.” David didn’t press when Dwight hesitated at the corridor, flashlight already trembling in his hand. He knew what was waiting there. They both did. But at the rate the water was rising, they were running out of time to debate routes. The pipe hallway had grown. There was no other explanation for it — the junctions multiplying, familiar valves appearing in unfamiliar arrangements, the walls presenting corners that hadn't existed on the first pass. The flashlight beam caught pipes and more pipes and the occasional burst of weirdly neutral- temperature spray as something gave way overhead, hosing them down without warning before the pressure died and the dark closed back in. The flashlight’s beam cut through the dark like a scalpel, but even in the narrow corridors it was weak. Sickly yellow and wavering, barely enough to outline the pipe-laced walls. Water was already brushing along their ribs now. For Dwight, it felt like it was pulling at him, rising along his stomach with a patient claiming. The water lower down tugged at his ankles lightly, a surreal current leading nowhere that felt determined to pull him away from the walls and back into the darkness. He wasn’t cold. Not really. But he still shook so badly he could hardly keep the light straight. It flickered against the walls as if it was afraid too. Every few steps, something slapped or hissed beside them, busted pipes still spewing from unseen seams. It felt personal. Like the building itself was spitting on them for trespassing. David squinted against it, pushing forward with grim determination. The floor was harder to grip as the water level rose, his own buoyancy making his feet slide slightly with every step. Every pipe they brushed against sent shivers up his spine. To his side, Dwight stumbled and nearly fell. David grabbed his arm without looking. The man may have been taller than him, but he was significantly less stable on his feet. Something brushed against Dwight’s leg again — lower, almost playful in its angle — causing a high sound that he hadn’t meant to make. He jolted. The flashlight spun. Water slapped. “David—” “Yeah, I feel it too.” David muttered. “Just keep moving.” They turned another corner. Somehow it was the same corner as the last one. It had to be. “I think we’re going in circles...” “No. We’re not. The pipes — look — they’re different here.” They weren’t. Neither man would admit it. They just adjusted their direction and pushed on. From somewhere above, the pipes hissed—and with a heavy thump, a jet of water slammed down like a burst fire hose into Dwight’s back, driving him into the wall. The flashlight went under for a second. He scrambled to fish it up off the floor, coughing as he surfaced. “Dwight!” “I’m fine!” It was half-truth, but he forced himself to believe it anyways. The light flicked back on just in time to see the hallway stretch again. The corridor behind them looked longer than before, the corner they had just turned already swallowed up in the dark. Dwight pushed water-soaked hair back from his face and steadied himself, pushing on to follow David down the hallway. And behind them, the water followed. Slow. Steady. Inevitable. The second-floor hallway was dry. Mostly. A few dark puddles gleamed near the warped window frames, but it hadn’t reached here yet. Not enough to matter. Danny lounged on the upper landing with all the practiced sprawl of a bored cat; one knee hooked over the balustrade and the other braced against the cracked drywall like a king surveying his flooded kingdom. His phone was in his hand, angled down, its screen throwing a faint glow up against his mask. His robes pooled around him, dry and settled, the long straps gently fluttering around him, as if She was enjoying the show by his side. Below him, the school was doing something genuinely impressive. He'd seen Her work before. Watched domains shift, watched geometry go quietly wrong in ways that took survivors too long to notice. But this was more deliberate than usual — the hallways stretching, the furniture piling itself well beyond the random junk he'd tossed down the stairs earlier, the water rising with that particular patient quality of something that had already decided how this ended and was just filling in the middle parts. She was definitely enjoying Herself tonight. That much was obvious. On the feed, a grainy-green lens tracked the survivors below. The RC submarine had been an impulse purchase — spotted in a novelty shop in someone's memory of a boardwalk, bought on the vague suspicion that it might be funny someday. He hadn't anticipated how funny. The camera he'd rigged to it wasn't anything special, cheap night vision that turned everything a washed-out green, but it was picking up every inch of Dwight Fairfield flinching away from something he couldn't see as he circled the man’s ankles like a curious shark, and that was frankly more than enough. The camera feed swayed with the current, too slow to track at first, until it bumped into something. He flicked the rudder, turned the camera angle, and watched as Dwight jumped again — probably thought he felt a tail. Danny snorted softly into the darkness. “Fucking priceless.” He zoomed in, casually, as Dwight flailed sideways into the wall, barely muffling his own shout. Every kick, every flail, every panicked gasp was caught on film. Poor quality, sure, but the emotions read clear. Fear didn’t need 4K. “Welcome back to Night Watch,” he murmured to no one, the corners of his mouth twitching in amusement. “I’m your host, Danny 'Fuck Around and Find Out' Johnson. Let’s check in on our contestants.” He stretched a little, back cracking. Took a lazy look down the hall through his phones own camera. The school was twisting all on its own now. He didn't need to chase them. Didn't need to do anything, really — She had renovated the entire school into something these two were never getting out of on their own, and all he had to do was sit here and document the experience. He even had night vision mode on his phone for if they eventually made it upstairs. He had footage already that was genuinely some of his best work. And somewhere below him, in the dark and the rising water, Dwight Fairfield was standing very still and trying very hard not to make any noise about whatever had just grazed his knee. He adjusted the camera angle one more time, getting a better view of the pipe hallway, and settled back against the wall with a comfortable sigh. Easiest trial he'd had in years. No knives today. No hooks. Just patience, petty vengeance, and a camera. And eventually, he would wander back to his safe spot for the night with a fantastic new film for his collection, while the Entity rested from the finest meal she’s had in ages. He adjusted the angle with a lazy finger flick and watched the chaos bloom below like algae, murky, aimless, choking. Chapter Three: Surface Tension The water had risen to their shoulders, making forward progress a tense, miserable slog. Dwight kicked gently to keep his head above the surface, the motion strange and clumsy. kept one hand on the pipes running along the wall, using them to pull himself forward against the current rather than fight it directly. It was slow, but it was the only thing keeping him upright. He was tall enough to stay grounded if he really stretched, but David wasn’t so lucky — the man was full-on treading water, eyes narrowed in concentration as he tried to keep from bumping into any more unseen furniture drifting beneath them. The current tugged at Dwight's legs, lazy and persistent, and his jacket clung to him like a wet towel, dragging him down. Every stroke felt heavier. Slower. The pockets were sodden, and the soaked fabric pulled at his arms as he reached for the pipes lining the walls, trying to orient himself. “This is stupid,” he muttered, breath ragged. “This is so stupid.” He reached for another pipe — nearly missed — and yanked himself sideways just in time to avoid colliding with a floating end-table. He grabbed the next pipe junction, steadied himself, and noticed that he was slower than he'd been ten minutes ago. Slower and lower. Somewhere behind him, David grunted. The sound was swallowed a little by the dark, but still audible. The flashlight’s beam — barely hanging on — flickered again as it caught on the edge of a floating chair, then skipped off into empty space. Something bumped against Dwight’s thigh. He didn’t scream. Couldn’t. His breath locked down hard in his chest, throat clenched. The water tugged at his legs with the slow pull of an undertow that didn’t belong in a hallway. He reached for a pipe, any pipe, his fingers scrabbling against wet metal. Another tug. The weight of his jacket had become unbearable. It sucked at his arms, pulled his body down, soaked cloth clinging against his skin. He gasped and fumbled with the zipper, yanking the jacket loose and letting it drift free in the water. It wasn’t that much of a loss — the Fog would return it at the campfire like everything else the survivors left behind — but he still felt exposed without it. The ceiling was maybe 2 feet above the water now, maybe less, the space between the surface and the plaster shrinking steadily. He kept his eyes on it anyway — not that looking helped, the flashlight beam barely reaching the pipes directly ahead of them — and tried not to think about what it meant that he could feel the cold air on the top of his head. The flashlight buzzed. The bulb flickered, dimmed, flared again like it was coughing. It had never been good, but the periodic submersions had taken something fundamental out of it — the beam guttering now when it should have held steady, throwing the ceiling into shadow for a half second at a time before catching again. Dwight held it above the surface as much as he could manage, which wasn't always, and every time it went under, he felt the weight of the dark press in a little closer. He was starting to lose track of where the hole should be. The hallway had shifted so much from its original shape that nothing lined up anymore — no landmark he'd clocked on the first pass was where he expected it to be, and the ceiling above them was uniform and featureless in the failing beam. What if She'd closed it? What if the geometry had swallowed it entirely, the way it had swallowed the extra distance and the extra junctions and the logic of the space itself? Dwight shook off the thought, blinked hard and adjusted the angle. He had been sweeping the ceiling in slow arcs, watching the plaster slide past in the weak yellow light, when the texture changed — torn edges framing a gap that swallowed the beam entirely, a circle of absolute black that stretched the full width of the hallway above them. “There!” he shouted, voice cracking with hope and desperation. “There it is!” David looked up with a half-relieved laugh just as the flashlight gave its last pathetic breath. A final, stuttering flick of yellow that haloed the hole for barely a second... And died. The dark swallowed them. No noise. No light. Just breath and water and the dizzying pressure of a space that no longer wanted them. “Shit – no no no...” Dwight shook the flashlight, trying to will it back to life. The current dragged at his hips and his elbow hit a pipe, the flashlight popping free of his grasp and lazily drifting towards the floor. “Dwight?” “I’ve got it! I—” He flailed, slipped under for a second, and broke the surface again coughing. David's hand found his collar and hauled him back up, hard enough to hurt. “You don’t got it,” David snapped. “I’m fine,” Dwight choked out, blinking water from his eyes. He could still see the hole in his mind — could still remember the angle — but now there was only black. "David, the light - I can't..." “Just leave it! Come on. The hole was right there. Feel around! It spanned the whole hallway. It’s not like we can miss it.” Dwight tipped his head back. The ceiling was right there — he could feel the cold air against his face, barely a foot of space between the water's surface and the plaster. He reached up and his fingers found it immediately. Dwight hesitated in the dark for a moment before slamming his palm against the ceiling, clinging to the pipes on the wall for stability as the two scrambled down the hall towards where they had last seen the edge. They moved by touch, hands flat against the ceiling, the current tugging at their legs with that same gentle insistence that had followed them through the whole hallway. Dwight counted his strokes. Fifteen feet, maybe less. They'd seen it. It was right there. The ceiling slid under his palms, unbroken and smooth, telling him nothing. — They went under together. One moment there was still an inch of air, the cold plaster brushing the tops of their heads, and then there wasn't — the surface closing the last gap with a quiet finality. No rush. No drama. Just the ceiling arriving, and the space gone, and the dark complete in every direction at once. The current had been waiting for exactly this — the moment neither of them had a surface to orient by — and it pulled with more confidence now, a slow lateral drag that had no interest in where they wanted to go. He kept one hand on the ceiling, pulling himself forward through the dark, counting his strokes the way he'd been counting since the flashlight died. The hole had been fifteen feet ahead, maybe less. He'd seen it. He knew where it was. At some point he realized he couldn't feel David anymore. Not a dramatic separation — no collision, no moment of loss. Just the gradual awareness that the presence he'd been tracking by sound and movement and the occasional brush of an arm had gone quiet, and the vibrations in the water were coming from somewhere he couldn't locate, muffled and directionless in the dark. He swept a hand out to the side and found nothing but water. Dwight didn’t mean to lose track of him. But the bizarre current, however slow it seemed, tugged him just wrong. Or maybe it was panic. Maybe it was the weight of soaked clothes and adrenaline twisting his limbs. One moment he was kicking toward the shape in the ceiling, lungs burning, hands scraping slick surfaces. The next, he was alone. Water above. Water below. No direction. No light. No grip. The water crawled into every seam of skin and clothing like a living thing. It pulsed in Dwight’s sinuses, hissed in his ears, beat against his ribcage with an endless roar. Panic surged. Dwight’s lungs seized. He forced himself not to inhale, not to kick too hard. He stayed close to the ceiling, one hand pressed flat against it, working along by feel alone. Plaster. Tile. Seam. Crack. Pipe— Nothing. Every sound dissolved into the water, tunneling awareness into vague thumps and creaks just out of range. A thud rolled through the water, metal on metal, distant. He twisted, bubbles clawing free from his throat. Another vibration, swallowed so fully it was more pressure than sound, rippling along his ribs. It might’ve been David. Might’ve been the pipes screaming again. He couldn’t tell. A pipe materialized where the hallway shouldn't have had one, catching his shoulder and spinning him partway around. He found the ceiling again and reoriented, except he wasn't certain anymore which direction he'd come from. The current pushed at his legs from a new angle. Something moved in the water nearby — too large to be debris, too deliberate — and grazed the back of his calf with the particular patience of something that had been following him for a while. Dwight kicked hard, arms scrabbling against walls that weren’t where they should be. His brain screamed up! but his body spun, panic shredding orientation until he didn’t know which way he was moving. The flashlight had been a compass, however weak, and now it was gone. Pressure gnawed at his ears. His chest locked, ribs straining for breath that wasn’t there. His vision prickled at the edges, the rising stars of a blackout dancing with every frantic movement. Something brushed past his leg again. Not a graze this time. Not the lazy curious arc of something circling. This was deliberate — a solid nudge against his calf that sent a shock of pure animal panic up his spine, and his body reacted before his brain could intervene. He jerked, twisting, bubbles tearing from his nose in a strangled choke, and for one disorienting heartbeat, he was sure there wasn’t a surface. Just water forever. His knuckles struck tile. Then hit a ridge. Broken ceramic. Something hard and sharp and... right. He clawed upward, fingers catching, dragging. His arms caught the edge of something, and he pulled. Up. Up. Some kind of splinter tore skin from his palm. His whole body surged, slamming shoulder-first into the gap. The world detonated. His throat ripped open around the first savage gasp, water and air fighting for space. He broke the surface gagging, hacking, shuddering so hard his knees buckled the instant he scrambled onto the sodden tiles. He curled onto his side, heaving, spit and floodwater streaming out of him in trembling bursts. He coughed until his ribs ached. Pressed his forehead to the floor. Breathed. The hallway was dark and quiet except for the soft lap of water against the edges of the hole behind him. Just the water. Just his shaking breaths. Dwight allowed the cool tiles to hold him, boneless, limbs jittering with aftershock. Relief hit sharp and dizzying; he’d found it, he was out, he was alive. He allowed himself to simply breathe against the cold tiles for a time. It took a minute to realize he was the only one doing so. He twisted back toward the hole, horror seizing his gut like a vice. "...David?" The sound cracked, raw, too small for the drowned dark. Nothing answered but the slap of water against ceiling. The tile was cold against his palms and his chest heaved and the water ran off him in thin streams and he waited for the sound of David breaking the surface behind him. Hands finding the edge. The grunt of effort. Something. The water lapped softly at the edges of the hole. It hadn’t even been that long, but David wasn’t there. The water churned quietly below him, but no head broke the surface. No splashing. No sign. His head buzzed from the pressure knotting in his chest. David had been right there. Right beside him. One selfish beat, he thought of staying out, curling in the puddle and pretending David would follow. His body screamed for it. He'll be right behind you. The thought came with the exhaustion, easy and warm and almost convincing. Just rest. Just breathe. He's coming. Dwight lay on the tile a moment more and breathed and listened to the silence. Then moved back to the hole. He found it by feel, fingers trailing across tile until the edge dropped away, and reached into the water up to his shoulder. Nothing. He swept his arm in a slow arc, searching, hoping to catch a fistful of sleeve, hair, something. Anything. The gentle tug of the current wrapped around his wrist, providing nothing in return. A swirl of movement shifted gently against the back of his hand and he leaned further in, focusing on the current. It wasn’t the same kind of tug on his skin. This felt focused — a deliberate movement rather than the flow that had knocked him around in the hallway. David’s close — Dwight realized in an instant — but he’s off course. The same current that tried to steal Dwight is dragging David too, just far enough to miss the exit. He was lost. The silence of the hallway pressed in expectantly. Like the floor was holding its breath, waiting to see if he’d move. Dwight swore he could hear the distant tick of settling tile, the whisper of water threading under the walls. The hole gently sloshed against his arm, simply waiting. He wasn’t going to find the edge. Dwight would have guide him. That meant going back in. He squeezed his eyes shut against the darkness, steeling himself as best he could, every nerve shrieking. He sucked one more shuddering breath and dove, black water swallowing him whole. It was so much worse the second time. His muscles were jelly, lungs scalded raw. Each stroke felt a half-second too slow. He swept his arms wide, blind, hands rasping pipe and plaster, mentally mapping the way back. The water pressure slammed into his body like a second impact, stealing the little air he had left. But he pushed through it, arms out, kicking hard. He followed the flow, felt for resistance. The movement was stronger now — more urgent, less controlled — and he knew what that meant. He'd been in enough trials to know what David panicking felt like. The movement thrashed ahead, strong, furious, off course. Dwight lunged, hand snagging something. Fabric. Arm. Elbow. The flail that followed would’ve knocked his teeth in if not for the drag of the water. He pulled. David pulled back on reflex, wrong direction, and Dwight held on and redirected, hand over hand up David's arm until he had him by the collar and could haul him bodily toward the ceiling. They surfaced together in a mess of limbs and swearing. David gasped like someone being born again, hair plastered to his face, arm curling tight against Dwight’s as they clawed for the edge. This time, it was David who found the lip, muscling them both up and over in a final, sodden scramble. They got out. That was the only thought Dwight's brain could hold for a while — the simple, enormous fact of tile under his hands and air above his head, real air, not a shrinking inch of it with water pressing in from below. He stayed down, pressed tight against solid ground, and coughed until his chest ached and then kept coughing anyway, because his lungs had opinions about the last several minutes and they were going to be heard. Somewhere beside him, David was doing the same. For a long, long moment, they didn’t move. Then David started laughing. For half a second, Dwight couldn’t tell if it was actually laughter or sobbing. His ears were still ringing from the silence below, and the sound scraped like a blade across bruised nerves. The deep hiccups of laughter broke the silence with a wheezing, exhausted lilt — helpless and a little broken at the edges and contagious in the specific way that delirious relief always was. Somehow, that made it real. They’d made it. Barely. Dwight answered with a grunt and flopped sideways on the cold tile, absolutely spent. “Next time,” David gasped through rawed-out chuckles, “you lead.” “Next time,” Dwight muttered, “I stay upstairs.” — THWACK. Dwight let out a sharp yelp of pain as something solid smacked into the side of his head. He blinked, vision swimming, catching a blur of movement and a sharp gasp and the scrape of boots on tile as whoever had hit him scrambled backward. A beam of light swung across them — strong and bright and absolutely blinding after hours of nothing — and Dwight threw an arm up against it, eyes watering. "Oh my god—" A voice. Female. Familiar. "Oh my god, I'm so sorry, I didn't see you, I almost—" David hissed and tried to turn away from the light, entirely too bright after all the darkness. The light veered quickly to one side with a trail of apologies, finally letting Dwight’s eyes adjust enough to see Orela — wild-eyed, nearly having walked straight into the hole they’d just escaped, were it not for the sudden human speed bump in the way. “Holy fuck,” Dwight choked, rubbing his eyes with a groan. “Warn a guy before kicking his brain back into his skull...” “Oh my god, I didn’t see you!” Orela stooped to help Dwight sit up. “We thought we heard something so I was just...how did you even get in here? What happened?” David coughed out another laugh. “Spent some time in the school’s new waterpark. I don’t recommend it.” Orela helped Dwight to sit upright, frowning as swept the flashlight over the two of them, taking in their state fully for the first time, soaked and wheezing on the floor. The beam passed over the hole and froze as realization sank in. “You guys were downstairs this whole time?” The three of them sat there, blinking in the flashlight glare, dripping onto the hallway floor as the silence of the preschool returned. Orela stared at the hole for a moment longer than was strictly necessary. The water lapped softly at its edges, dark and patient, like it was waiting to see if anyone else was going to come back for it. "Right," she said, in the tone of someone filing several things away to process later. She crouched down and got a hand under Dwight's arm, helping him upright. He came up slowly, waterlogged and unsteady. "Sorry about your head," she said. "S'fine," Dwight managed. It wasn't entirely fine. But it was fine enough. David got himself up without assistance through what appeared to be sheer principle, made it to vertical, and stayed there through an act of will that Orela clocked but didn't comment on. She cast one last look at the hole in the floor before turning away. The three of them moved off into the dark of the hallway, wet footsteps marking the tile behind them. Behind them, the water lapped quietly at the edge of the hole. Rising, still. Patient as anything. Chapter Four – Echo Chamber The classroom Orela led them to was small even by the school's original standards — low desks, scattered toys, cabinets with chipped paint. It looked ordinary enough. That was almost worse. The school she'd navigated to find them bore almost no resemblance to the building they'd entered. Hallways that should have been thirty feet were closer to a
